facts.statement: Wilaru lived in Australia during the Late Oligocene to Early Miocene, approximately 26 to 22 million years ago.
facts.quote: Wilaru is an extinct genus of presbyornithid bird from Australia during the Late Oligocene to Early Miocene, around 26-22 million years ago.

facts.statement: The type species Wilaru tedfordi was discovered in the Namba Formation of the Lake Eyre Basin in north-eastern South Australia.
facts.quote: The type species, Wilaru tedfordi, was described from fossil material collected from Lake Pinpa, Lake Palankarinna and Billeroo Creek, specifically in the Namba Formation of Lake Eyre Basin, north-eastern South Australia.

facts.statement: The genus name Wilaru means "stone curlew" in the Diyari language.
facts.quote: The genus name Wilaru is the term for "stone curlew" in the Diyari language of the Lake Eyre region.

facts.statement: The species name tedfordi honors Richard H. Tedford, who led the 1971 expedition that collected the fossil material.
facts.quote: The specific epithet of the type species W. tedfordi honours American palaeontologist Richard H. Tedford (1929–2011) of the American Museum of Natural History, who led the 1971 expedition to Lake Pinpa during which much of the descriptive material was collected.

facts.statement: The holotype of Wilaru tedfordi is a left humerus, and the holotype of Wilaru prideauxi is a right tarsometatarsus.
facts.quote: The holotype of W. tedfordi is a left humerus (SAMA P48925), while the holotype of W. prideauxi is a right tarsometatarsus (SAMA P53136).

facts.statement: Wilaru was specialized for a more terrestrial lifestyle compared to other presbyornithids, as indicated by its tarsometatarsal morphology.
facts.quote: Compared to other presbyornithids, Willaru appeared to have been specialised to a more terrestrial lifestyle, based on its tarsometatarsal morphology.

facts.statement: Wilaru prideauxi was larger and more robust than Wilaru tedfordi, suggesting a specialization toward a terrestrial lifestyle.
facts.quote: In particular, the latter W. prideauxi appears to have been more specialised towards terrestriality than the earlier W. tedfordi, being larger and more robust, indicating a clear speciation towards this lifestyle and therefore a direct species sequence.

facts.statement: Wilaru possessed spurs and knobs on its carpals, similar to modern waterfowl.
facts.quote: Like many modern waterfowl, the Willaru species had spurs and knobs on their carpals.

facts.statement: The spurs and knobs on Wilaru were likely used for fighting and territorial behavior, unlike the gregarious habits of earlier presbyornithids.
facts.quote: Like the closely related modern-day screamers, these were almost certainly used to fight, indicating perhaps territorial habits, as opposed to the more gregarious nature of earlier presbyornithids.

facts.statement: Wilaru coexisted with various anatid and anseranatid species with little ecological competition.
facts.quote: Willaru co-existed with several anatid and anseranatid species, indicating that there was little ecological competition.

facts.statement: A 2025 study based on a nearly complete skull of Vegavis confirmed Wilaru as a member of the Presbyornithidae family within Anseriformes.
facts.quote: However, a 2025 study which reported a nearly complete skull of Vegavis revised the phylogenetic analyses of Galloanserae and recovered Wilaru as a member of the Presbyornithidae within Anseriformes.

facts.statement: The fossil record of Wilaru spans from the Chattian to the Burdigalian stages, between 27.3 and 15.98 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Chattian to Burdigalian (27.3 to 15.98 million years ago)

rejected.quote: The second species, Wilaru prideauxi, was first named in 2016 after the Australian vertebrate paleontologist Gavin Prideaux.
